reasoning: The only woman is the biblical Shunamite, cited inside the tzaddik's exegetical homily (her testing of Elisha's sheets) rather than acting in the story itself, so she is referred to but not a narrative actor.

The story defends the Besht's honor and says common people should not judge disputes between tsaddikim, but it does not depict cleaving to or receiving from a tsaddik, faith in the tsaddik, or a tsaddik interceding for others.

The only relative who appears is R. Gershon, the Besht's brother-in-law, who is extended rather than immediate family (wife, children, parents), though he does play an active role in healing and testing the visitor.
The story shows a dead man's spirit (ruach/dybbuk) possessing a madwoman and being expelled, which is spirit possession rather than reincarnation of a soul into a new life.

R' Yitzhak is depicted acting as a sofer: he checks the man's tefillin, finds them invalid, and writes new tefillin parchments for him, boasting that he never wrote tefillin like these, which implies scribal practice, though his profession is not stated outright.

The Besht's blessing (with the threat of breaking her bones with his staff) causes the previously sonless wife to bear a son that year — a discrete wonder with a clear before/after attached to the recipients, followed by the foretold loss of his wealth.
The Besht laughs at R. Gershon and at the end says jokingly (בדרך שחוק) to his followers "beat him so he won't laugh at the Besht," which is an explicit jest by the tsaddik.

The Besht sees the expelled spirit (קליפה) as a giant Cossack by the gate, which shrinks and vanishes as he approaches, a vision of an unseen demonic presence, though the story centres more on protective amulets and exorcism.

The story shows the land-shochet testing slaughterers on the laws and the knife (the notched-knife test). It also shows a legal ruling: the Spoler Zeide as dayyan permitted an agunah, the rabbis forbade her, and the case went through she'elot u-teshuvot.

The heiress repeatedly ignores the tzaddik's instruction to marry the man from Lutsk, even after a dream warning, and falls deathly ill until she submits, which is disobedience with consequences, though it comes as a retrospective subplot.

The story is explicitly framed as the Besht's revelation (התגלותו) and culminates in his public emergence at 36: he heals the madman, leaves teaching, takes a scribe, and people travel to him from everywhere.

The only storytelling here is the generic frame 'R. Pesach told me', a transmission formula, and no telling of tales is depicted as a practice at a gathering, a meal or a set occasion; the story itself is a miracle tale about the Besht lighting a tree.
The story contrasts ascetic immersion with the Besht's method for overcoming alien thoughts; it does not depict cleaving to a tsaddik, faith in the tsaddik, or a tsaddik interceding for others.

Most of the story takes place while the Besht lives in the village, but its ending turns on his journey: travelling through a forest with companions, he stops, sees the imprisoned demon, laughs, and tells the tale.

The Besht says he prayed in the mikveh and asked why the matter had been hidden from him, and 'they answered me' (השיבו לי) that it was a punishment for neglecting a scholar's eulogy, which is an exchange with heavenly beings; his hearing the court's talk from afar is clairvoyance rather than contact with invisible beings.

The searchers look under the very bed where the three tzaddikim are hiding and miraculously fail to see them (explained by the eggs and produce serving as a pidyon), which is a discrete supernatural rescue; the later mention of מופתים is only ambient.

R. Shmeril's shame is explicit (מפני הבושה, ובוש ממנו) and drives the plot: it stops him from asking for a son until the Besht anticipates the request, though this is bashful embarrassment rather than being shamed as a consequence.

R' Shmeril customarily traveled to the Besht after each birth to get an amulet, and the story shows him making that journey after his son's birth, where the Besht tells him he chose a son over wealth for him.

The Besht's family members here are his brothers-in-law (R. Gershon and R. Yaakov), not the wife, children or parents the definition specifies, although both are active characters, so a broader reading of the tag could include them.

The story centres on Jews arrested in the Pavolitch blood libel (called השבוים); the Besht repeatedly prays for their deliverance and is promised the decree's annulment, and a Brody preacher who exploited the captives for money is blamed for their deaths, so efforts to free the prisoners are part of the plot, though no ransom is actually paid.

The story's climactic event, the rebbe's release from prison by Tsar Alexander, is explicitly dated to 29 Kislev, the fifth candle of Chanukah, so a key event takes place on the holiday, though Chanukah plays no further thematic role.

The story centres on the Besht's clairvoyance about the toll collector's death; the toll collector's suspicion, R. Gershon's rebuke and the mockery of R. Yaakov are brief frictions, not a depicted conflict with an antagonist.

R. Gershon's self-deprecating remark ('would that I had the world to come the Besht earns from one pipe') mainly serves to exalt the Besht, and the second tale is about the Besht's seemingly improper anger, so humility is not depicted as a virtue in its own right.

The story narrates the Besht's revelation (hitgalut): at 36 he is told his time has come, starts receiving supplicants, gives up teaching, takes a scribe, and people travel to him from everywhere, which is his assumption of public leadership, though there is no formal installation ceremony.

The Rav sees that Paul 'has no form of an emperor' 30 days before his murder, senses the news of the death 'through divine wisdom' before the bells are heard, and later reveals the assassins to Alexander, which is clear supernatural perception.

R. Gershon of Kitov's scorn and his attempt to have the madwoman expose the Besht is skeptical hostility toward a concealed tzaddik, not a contest between rival tzaddikim; the rain episode with the gentiles' idols is a brief side comparison, not a depicted rivalry.

The beit midrash and the kloyz in Brody are only mentioned: the two men go off to wait there, and the Besht sends money to its members and says he saw the Shekhinah resting on it. The scenes themselves take place at the inn and on the road.

The Ruzhiner stands absorbed in prayer at kiddush levana for about five hours, unaware of the time and the guard's mortal danger, and 'awakens' only at the end, which depicts rapt absorption in God, though the story's focus is the miracle protecting the soldier.

The Besht performs discrete supernatural acts: the demon cannot enter his four cubits, he sends it back to harm the witch, and he binds it forever in a forest prison, which he later shows his companions. The rain itself is never shown falling, and the witch's sorcery belongs under supernatural:magic.

The Besht's prescription turns the son from a wild, unteachable child into 'another man' devoted to Torah, which is a spiritual transformation of the son, though it happens offstage and no explicit tikkun or repentance is shown.

The only clothing details are a passing note that R. Mendel sat in Sabbath clothes at R. Nahman's deathbed and that Nahman prayed without tallit and tefillin, which are ritual-object details rather than clothing with thematic significance.

The story raises whether one may speak mundane or foreign languages on Shabbat and concludes with a ruling ('מותר לדבר אף בלשונות העמים בשבת'), though the ruling rests on a homiletical and spiritual argument rather than formal legal sources, and the scholars' test is on a midrash, not on law.
The rabbi of Lutsk travels to the Besht to ask for a son and again to invite him to be sandek, and the shochet finally travels to the Besht to confess and seek penance.

The story centers on a man in Kutov who constantly spoke against the Hasidic fellowship, quarreled with R. Aharon and tore his beard, was excommunicated by R. Gershon, and the posthumous consequences of this opposition drive the plot.

The Besht only says hypothetically that he could have drawn down Adam's soul for his son 'in the secret of ibbur'; no soul is actually shown being reincarnated, and the story centers on his deathbed exchange with his son.

The rain that stranded the rabbi stops at once when he agrees to keep Shabbat in the town, a discrete providential event with a clear before and after, though the Besht's knowing from afar and his prophecy count only as ambient wonder-working.
R. Nahman, a tsaddik, is passing through Zolkiew on a trading journey, and the whole story turns on that stop: he halts his wagon at the beit midrash and leads the prayers uninvited as a stranger.

When the attendant hears the dead klezmer's voice, the story shows physical trembling in response to the supernatural: 'ורוב עצמותיו הפחידו וברכיו דא לדא נקשין' (his bones shook and his knees knocked together), and he later shakes with fear at the shrouded figure.

In the final episode the Besht sees הס"ם (Samael) on the road waiting to seize the Yom Kippur prayers and has to route them around him; Samael acts here as an accuser who traps prayers rather than as a bringer of death, but the tag definition explicitly includes סמאל.

The story centres on Alexander Shohet's years as the Besht's scribe and protégé: the Besht places him in posts, sends him to exorcise a spirit, comforts him afterwards, and admonishes him through the Garden of Eden vision.

The tailor deceives the queen with an invented story about the second earring to expose the bishop, whose claim to fly to Muhammad's grave is itself a fraud he admits, and the bishop then lies to the crowd that the earring proves he made the flight.
The scribe drives off the spirit himself with holy names. The Besht only sends him on the exorcism and afterward tells him not to fear, so he does not shield anyone from harm.

Two Chabad hasidim visit R. Aharon of Karlin for Shabbat; he seats and honors them as guests at his table, then tests and rebukes them for their lack of humility, which is a depiction of the tsaddik receiving and testing visitors at his court.

The Spoler Zeide deliberately deceives twice: he nicks a perfect knife and falsely claims he sharpened it to test the drunk examiner, and he lures the host to the window by pretending to have a secret to reveal.

The story shows a visiting tzaddik explaining the Saba's nut game to his own followers (a master-disciple exchange) and the Saba's dancing moving onlookers to repentance; there is no real interaction among Hasidim as peers.

The plot turns on Jewish law: a beit din coerces and issues a get written 'according to halakhah', the 91-day waiting period before remarriage is observed, the tzaddik judges the get invalid and invokes the legal presumption that no one brazenly claims a debt not owed, and the woman turns out to still be legally married.

The story centres on hasidim streaming to the Seer of Lublin and the tsaddik's prophetic power over a man's fate, and it explicitly weighs the tsaddik's power against that of the hasidic collective ('what ten hasidim can do, one holy tsaddik cannot'), so the doctrine of the tsaddik is thematised rather than incidental.

The young man begs to be drawn close to the rebbe and sacrifices all his wealth to join his circle, and the tsaddik (R. Leib Sarahs) then secretly arranges his fortune and his true match, so that the couple were 'like clay in the potter's hand' in the rebbe's hands.
The story depicts litigants coming before R. Yitzhak for judgment (באו לדין), with a ruling imposing an oath, i.e. an actual halakhic court proceeding.

The Besht heals the blind boy's sight instantly by whispering holy names (he then reads a Gemara) and immediately reverses the cure — a discrete supernatural event with a clear before/after attached to the recipient.
The central scene takes place at a circumcision feast (סעודת ברית מילה) at a rich man's house, and the baal habrit is the one who strikes R. Mordechai, so the brit meal is the story's actual setting.

The story is about the Ruzhiner's imprisonment and miraculous Kiddush Levanah, and the closing transmission note (heard from a reliable man via the attendant) is a provenance formula, not a depicted storytelling practice or occasion.
The rabbi's prayer and hand gesture strike Zusman's wife: she stands frozen like a stone and then dies, a discrete supernatural punishment-miracle with a clear before and after.

The townspeople ask about Rabbi Shmelke's puzzling private greeting to himself and he explains it on the spot; this is a solicited explanation of strange behavior, not a belated realization of a hidden truth about a person or event.

The tsadikim are laughed at and one is slapped at the circumcision feast, but this is ridicule they court as part of their wandering in disguise, and the drunken examiner is never exposed, so no character is shamed as a consequence.
Rabbi Nachman explicitly tells a mashal about two ministers arguing over how to set the stone in the king's crown, which forms the core structure of the story.

The story centres on the Besht's power to intercede: his tears shake all the heavenly palaces, his decree binds the martyred saints until they beg him to annul it, and heaven hid the decree because his prayer would have cancelled it.

The hidden tzaddik R. Leib, working as a lowly shamash in Zlatopol, is later recognized by the townspeople as 'a holy man of God', and R. Michel of Zlotchov likewise senses the disguised wanderer's true stature only after blessing him.

One episode (R. Michel of Zlotchov blessing people after Kabbalat Shabbat) is set on Shabbat eve, but it is a single short scene in a long biographical story about the Shpoler Zeide's concealment that otherwise does not center on Shabbat.

The Belz tsaddik intercedes and acts on others' behalf: he foresees the danger and urges confession, rescues the Jews by appearing in dreams to a gentile, and helps that gentile find his horses; the closing moral explicitly calls for strengthening faith in tsaddikim.
The story explicitly depicts the death of one of the lying litigant's children ('שמת אחד מזרעו') as the consequence that leads him to confess.
The closing tradition names a darshan in Brody, distinct from the Besht, whose sermon stirred strife and caused the captives' deaths; he appears only briefly but plays a decisive causal role.
The Besht is shown performing a unification ('וייחד עליה להחיצונים') to subdue the impure forces in the haunted house, and the story also mentions his use of holy names, though both are brief.
The townspeople are puzzled by Rabbi Shmelke honoring himself aloud, which looks like honor-seeking, and only after his explanation do they realize the hidden meaning and that he is a holy tzaddik.

The Rebbe's refusal of non-kosher food in prison is religious steadfastness under duress rather than resisting a temptation such as lust, profit or fame, and the officer not touching the jam is incidental.

The key scene takes place on Friday (עש"ק), when the tzaddik takes the arendar's last coins meant for Shabbat candles, brandy and kiddush wine, and the action resumes after Shabbat, so erev Shabbat frames the story's turning point.

Besides the rain-making through play, the story says everyone who saw the Saba's holy Sabbath dance returned in repentance (חוזר בתשובה), so the tsaddik draws onlookers to teshuva, though only as a brief general statement.

The story centres on the Besht's disciple (the Mochiach) winning over Lemberg's non-Hasidic establishment: the parnas, the town rabbi and the mocking local youths. The rabbi ends up endorsing the Besht and supporting the disciple, which is a substantive interaction with non-Hasidic Jews, though not with declared opponents.
The shochet's ongoing sexual sin with his daughter-in-law, which he attributes to his yetzer hara, is the hidden transgression that the Besht detects and that the plot turns on.

The Besht prolongs his Minha prayer until nightfall, standing and trembling with intense movements while performing kavvanot of unifications, and R. Gershon faints when he attempts the same kavvanah, which depicts ecstatic, absorbed prayer.

The central event is R. Shmelke's installation and reception as rabbi (av beit din) of Nikolsburg, where he rehearses the townspeople's greetings in private to guard against pride; this is a communal rabbinate rather than a rebbe's court, hence medium confidence.

The tsaddik deliberately disguises himself in a poor man's clothes (התחפש בבגדי עני) to conceal his holiness, and that poor dress is why the doorkeepers turn him away at R. Mordechai's door, so clothing carries social and religious meaning in the plot.

Glasses of wine set before the narrator by the Seer of Lublin crack and spill on their own, one after another, which reads as a discrete wondrous event tied to the narrator's refusal to drink, though the text never names it a נס or מופת.

The Besht's fervent prayer is shown concretely: he immerses in the mikveh even in the Tevet frost, and during prayer drops of sweat 'like beans' pour from him, a classic image of hitlahavut, though it is one detail within a longer revelation narrative.

At the circumcision feast the wandering tzaddikim publicly proclaim R. Mordechai as rabbi of Nishchiz and R. Yaakov as shatz of Zaslav, are mocked for it, and within days R. Mordechai is appointed rabbi of Nishchiz; this reads as foreknowledge, though it could also be read as a plan they agreed on among themselves.

Anger is explicitly depicted twice: the wife is angry at the leaseholder for spending the Sabbath money (כעסה עליו אשתו), and the other bidders' anger (חרה להם) drives their conspiracy against him, though neither is the story's central theme.

The shadchan explicitly flares up in anger ('מאשר חרה לו'), thinking the young man is mocking him, and the heiress's servants want to harm the newcomer until she tells them to restrain themselves; these are depicted heated moments, though secondary to the matchmaking plot.
A scribe (הסופר) is mentioned only once as sleeping in the wagon and plays no part in the miracle of the burning tree, so his presence is incidental.

R. Yitzhak's reply that he will enter the town just as the tax-farmer's bier is carried out toward him is fulfilled exactly at the gate, a pivotal fulfilled prediction, though the story is framed mainly around curse, controversy and punishment.

The central narrative is the Besht exposing a planted corpse meant for a blood libel against the Jews, protecting the community from hostile authorities, though he works by following and witnessing rather than by an active intervention.

R. Yitzchak's clairvoyance makes R. Birakh realize, after some sixty years, that his tefillin were invalid from the start, so he never truly fulfilled the mitzvah. That is a belated recognition about a past situation, though the story's main focus is the clairvoyance itself.
The story explicitly describes the tzaddik dancing on Sabbaths and festivals 'בהתלהבות ובהתפעלות עצומה', light-footed like a child, with his fervor moving onlookers to repentance.
The young woman's near-fatal illness pressures her into the destined match rather than punishing a wrongdoing, and the avrekh's poverty and his wife's death are trials, not retribution.

The innkeeper describes his wife pressing, inciting and cursing him to take a business partner during their poverty, and his reply to her that he had found a 'good partner', which shows a husband-wife dynamic, though only as a secondary episode.
While awake, the youth sees a disembodied talking head (the teraphim) and then sees his dead grandfather ('חזה העלם בעיניו את זקנו הנפטר') come and carry him home through the window.

The story is mainly about how the Besht was revealed, but the rain episode, where he tells the tenant farmer to inform the gentile that rain will fall that day and 'so it was', is a full episode built on a tzaddik's prediction that comes true.

The tax-farmer's wife seizes the butcher's bedding, the butcher's wife complains, and the curse and child's death that follow set off the feud between R. Yitzhak and the tax-farmer, a conflict the women then play no part in.
The congregants are puzzled by the Maggid's unfamiliar Lekha Dodi melody, and only after the shamash tells them about the dead klezmer do they realize its hidden meaning as a tikkun for his soul.

The story has R. Shmelke's exegesis of the dictum 'let your fellow's honor be dear to you as your own,' given as his teaching, followed by an extended homiletic discourse on R. Eliezer's charge to his students that resolves an apparent contradiction.

The story's climax reveals the confessor was the gilgul of Ishmael ben Netaniah, who killed Gedaliah, explaining his inexplicable hatred and his deserved death, so reincarnation is central to the plot.
The Besht foils the judge's blood-libel plot (a planted dead child hidden under his floor to frame the Jews) by publicly exposing it, a clear tzaddik-vs-non-Jewish-antagonist conflict.
The Besht trembles at night ('חרד הבעש״ט וארכובותיו דא לדא נקשן'), loudly enough to wake R. Zvi Sofer, in response to a visitation from his master and a spiritual warning.

The Rebbe interacts extensively with non-Jewish officials: the gendarme who falls at the sight of his tefillin and then pleads with him, and the fortress general who comforts him and personally fetches him kosher food.

The Besht reads the doctor's pulse and exposes him as the thief of the duke's long-missing valuables, so the duke belatedly learns who stole them, though the story's focus is the Besht's clairvoyant exposure rather than recognition as such.

The plot turns on vidui: the tsaddik recites and explains the liturgical Ashamnu formula, and the travelers later cry out to God and confess when stranded in the mud, though their confession is more spontaneous than formal liturgy.

When the shochet is caught, the text says he 'נתמלא רתת... וחלחלה' and cannot speak, physical trembling at the exposure the Besht foresaw; but it is mainly guilt and fear at being caught, so it fits the religious/supernatural sense only partly.

Young Shalom of Belz visits R. Uri of Strelisk's court, privately sets out to test whether he is a true rebbe, and the tsaddik rebukes the test before he accepts him as his teacher; this depicts a newcomer's arrival and testing.
Reb Leib, a Hasidic spy among the Gaon's people, hides his identity and is explicitly afraid of exposure ("כי ירא ר׳ ליב פן יודע הדבר"), and this fear of danger drives his secrecy and distress.

The story shows R. Mordechai of Neskhiz's court, where doorkeepers turn the poorly dressed Spoler Zeide away until the tsaddik recognizes his voice and has him admitted for a private audience; earlier, R. Michal of Zlotchov blesses visitors one by one, has the Zeide sought out, welcomes him and sends him on his way.

In the second story the Besht explains that his anger at his servant over the horse was a deliberate act: by casting fear on the servant he struck fear into robbers far away, so they left a Jew traveling on the road alive. This is a tsaddik shielding someone from mortal danger by mystical means.

The story centers on R. Shmelke's arrival and installation as rabbi (av beit din) of Nikolsburg and his conduct before the community's formal welcome; it is a communal rabbinic post rather than Hasidic kabbalat malkhut as rebbe, hence medium confidence.
The story ends by stating the Besht took the narrator's father-in-law, its main informant (R. Alexander), as his sofer, an explicit scribal role, though it is mentioned only briefly.

The witch is the Besht's main antagonist and acts on her own: she casts spells to stop the rain, goes twice to his mother to threaten him, and sends her demon against him, while his mother also intervenes to warn her son.

The only storytelling element is the narrator's chain of transmission (heard from the Zlotopoler rabbi, from his father, from the Spoler Zeide himself); no tale is told at a gathering, a meal or a set occasion, and none is told as a spiritual act.
The rebbe, while travelling, lodges with a follower in a village, and the whole story (the horse, the debt note, the reincarnated debtor) unfolds during this stay along the way.

The Saba of Shpola reproaches R. Mordechai of Neskhiz for breaking their agreement ('לא כן היה המדובר בינינו'), and they are overheard needling each other ('קנטרו זה לזה'), but this friction between two tzaddikim is brief and may be friendly rather than a real dispute.

The story centres on audiences at the Belz court: the leaseholder comes with his daughter and the groom, struggles to get access, is told cryptically to confess, and is dismissed, and the gentile wagoner's own audience, where he is made to promise to befriend Jews, drives the rescue.

The disguised 'merchants' are non-Jewish priests (כומרים) who work sorcery: they kill a prodigy every eighty years, put impure names from Jeroboam's teraphim under the severed head, and use it as an oracle, though the text never uses the word מכשף.
The Besht sees Sender in a heavenly vision of Gan Eden and immediately comes to reassure him about the night-time spirit attack, implying he knew of it without being told.

The narrator's father-in-law, Alexander Shohet, serves as a shohet in Berdichev, and the Besht's letter gets him appointed shohet u-bodek in Nemirov, an appointment within the shohet institution; however, this is framing biography and the core story is the Besht's vision and the fingernail episode.

The story centres on a hostile confrontation between the Jewish community and a non-Jewish antagonist: the duke decrees their destruction after an assassination attempt, and the confessor faces him and is executed, though no tzaddik is involved.

The leaseholder does not understand why the tzaddik urges him to confess; only when sinking in the swamp does he recall the words, and the peasant's account then shows the tzaddik foresaw the danger and sent the rescue, revealing the hidden meaning of the earlier exchange.

The rich man's wife despises the Besht because he is not wearing distinguished clothes (worn from travel), so his dress carries social significance and sets off the plot's central conflict, though it is mentioned only briefly.

The story is set around a dated local decree (year [5]396, Berezhnitz) by the duke to destroy the town's Jews after an assassination attempt, recorded in a communal pinkas; this fits the tag's 'decree' sense, though it is a local event rather than a widely known one.
The story opens with Shmelke's arrival and festive reception as rabbi of Nikolsburg, the community going out to greet and install him, and his conduct at that installation is the core of the tale.

R. Sh. learns only afterward that the trembling stove and chair came from a hidden visit by the Besht and the Maggid, and the rabbi identifies the unfamiliar Besht by inference; both are borderline, since the identification happens during the visit rather than after it.
The opening 'I heard from R. Aharon who told it before our rabbi' is a standard chain-of-transmission formula, with no depicted gathering, festive meal, set occasion or theurgic use of storytelling.

The story depicts the court of R. Mordechai of Neskhiz: crowds from all corners thronging his door, door-guards turning the poor visitor away, a gabbai opening for him and a private audience in a separate room, and it ends with R. Leib settling in Spola where people travel to him.
A non-Jewish woman (ארמית) is referred to as the son-in-law's illicit partner on the bed, and the Besht's clairvoyance hinges on this, but she never appears or acts in the story.
The Besht is repeatedly depicted in ecstatic, trembling prayer, with a burning face, fixed eyes, and being 'not in this world', which is a direct portrayal of rapt absorption in God.
The rebbetzin drives the plot: she quarrels with the maidservant, decides to sue her in court, and argues with her husband, even though the story's moral centers on the rabbi's response.
The Besht, while awake and far away, reports that he 'saw the ascent of the soul' (ראיתי עליות נשמתו) of a deceased tzaddik and recognized its movements, a supernatural waking sight.

The sinful shochet is providentially exposed, jailed by the community leaders, and forced to confess publicly, which is punishment for his wrongdoing, though it comes from the community rather than directly from Heaven or the tzaddik.

The man twice travels to R. Michal of Zlotshov, first arriving on the appointed day to be sent off and later journeying to report his experience and ask about the ownerless money, though the story's main journey is to the wealthy man in Berdichev.

At the circumcision feast the tzaddikim publicly hail R. Mordechai as 'rabbi of Neshkhiz' and are mocked and beaten for it, and the story then relates that he soon became av beit din there, so the prediction-and-fulfilment structure is a central arc, though the rest of the story concerns their escape and the Sabba's later career.

The only ascetic element is the shochet's passing remark that he performed great mortifications (סיגופים) in penitence; the Besht's refusal to eat is about non-kosher meat, not self-denial, so asceticism is incidental rather than a theme.

The Besht does relieve his freezing companions, but the story centres on the wonder of lighting a tree with his finger (and forbidding R. Baruch to look back), not on protecting someone from a threat like illness, hostile authorities or demons.
The narrator travels to the Seer of Lublin for Shabbat, and the whole episode with the cups of wine takes place at the Friday-night (ליל ש״ק) table.

The only related element is a brief formulaic line that the community fasted and 'cried out to God' (גזרו צום וקראו אל ה׳ בחזקה), which is incidental communal supplication rather than a depicted recitation of liturgy; the story centres on the self-sacrificing confessor and his reincarnation.

The story depicts the tsaddik praying inwardly while playing with children and dancing on Sabbaths and festivals in intense ecstasy (התלהבות והתפעלות עצומה), which is ecstatic worship and absorption in God.

The episode belongs to the Hasidim's campaign to free the imprisoned Rav (Shneur Zalman): R. Leib is sent to Vilna with money to gather intelligence on the opponents' efforts, and the story centres on the Rav's written defence and his expected release from prison.

The Besht's unexplained refusal to heal R. Yosef takes on its hidden meaning only after the apparent recovery ends in sudden death, when he reveals the heavenly proclamation he had heard, so the townspeople belatedly understand the situation.
A litigant makes a false claim (טען שקר) before the rabbinic court and is prepared to swear to it, then later confesses the truth, so lying is central to the plot.

The story centers on the tzaddik's tallit and his concern that its tzitzit be spun for the sake of the commandment, a ritual garment with explicit religious significance, though the focus is the fringes' ritual validity rather than dress as such.

The only trembling is the formulaic 'רעדה אחזתם', which is the community's fear of a blood libel, a worldly threat rather than a religious or supernatural response, and the Besht's fiery ecstasy involves no trembling.

The rabbi of Rashkov travels to the Besht for the Sabbath (פ"א נסע הרב לבעש"ט על שבת), is held up by rain in Sharigrad, and then arrives at the Besht after the Sabbath, so the journey is central to the plot.

The story depicts a discrete miracle: the pursuers search under the bed and fail to see the hidden tzaddikim, which the Spoler Zeide attributes to the eggs and produce serving as a pidyon (and to his own concealment without one); the general mention of R. Mordechai's 'awesome wonders' is only ambient.

The rabbi (R. Leib) habitually journeys to the great fairs and stays there, and the story turns on what he does during that stay: he gives a tikkun to a wandering dead soul, which explains the purpose of his travels.

Rabbi Leib Sarah's is explicitly a wanderer (נע ונד) lodging six weeks with an arendator in Bonitch, and the story turns on his stay there and his miraculous weekly journeys to Vienna, before moving on to Ladmir.

The tsaddik travels to the nobleman of Rashkov and the story turns on the prayer he says on the road, though this is a single errand trip rather than wandering or lodging with disciples or innkeepers.
Rabbi Nachman is explicitly described as becoming very angry ("והיטב חרה לו עד מאד") at those speaking against the Baal Shem Tov, and the parable's ministers rebuke the bystander angrily.

The story ends with the Besht rebuking R' Baruch for looking back at the miraculously burning tree, a taboo against looking like Lot's wife; it is a command not to do something, though a mystical taboo rather than a halakhic or moral prohibition.

The story turns on the halakhic requirement that tzitzit be spun lishmah, raising doubt over whether purchased tzitzit are valid, though the Besht resolves it by spiritual perception rather than legal ruling.

R. Leib Sarah's, the archetypal wandering nistar, is the central character: the innkeeper treats him as an unknown madman, and he works secretly, appearing at night as an anonymous 'old Jew' to bring back the servant, though the story never explicitly labels him a hidden tzaddik.

The main theme is the tikkun of the dead klezmer's soul, but the Maggid also protects the soul from the destroyers waiting outside by sending his attendant to escort it, and gives the attendant his staff to remove his fear.

The plot turns on the law of forgetting Ya'aleh ve-Yavo in the Rosh Hodesh prayer, and the Besht's insight that the parnas forgot it twice while praying, so prayer is both discussed and depicted as a central element.

Gentiles in Zaslav try to frame the Jews for a corpse found in a field (a blood libel) before the duchess, and the Besht defeats the threat through prayer in the mikveh; the story also includes a sharp exchange with the local rabbi.

The beit midrash appears only in a single summarizing clause (the impoverished avrekh sat studying there for a year), while every scene in the story takes place in his shop, the inn in Volkovishk, or the heiress's home.

The story shows a peer exchange between two Hasidic figures, R. Mordechai of Chernobyl as sandak and R. Avraham as mohel, with R. Mordechai questioning him about his awe, rather than a master-disciple relationship.
The passage is a hearsay report ('we heard from our master') about a circumcision episode, with no tale told at a gathering or meal and no storytelling used as a spiritual act.
The Besht explicitly speaks 'בבדיחותא' to the fainting melamed, quipping that he would hardly be so moved by something new, since he had already heard it all in his dream.

The tzaddik's curse suddenly strikes the innkeeper's wife and sons with illness and is lifted when he obeys, and the lost servant is miraculously brought back overnight to save the accused Jew; both are discrete miracles with clear before/after.

The Besht's clairvoyant exposure of the shochet's hidden sin leads the shochet to confess before him and beg for a penance (tikkun teshuva), although the story's main focus is exposing the sin and vindicating the Besht, and the repair itself is only briefly noted.
R. Samson Wertheimer stays in Vienna and others travel to him; his single wagon trip to officiate at the wedding is a destination visit where the exposure happens, not wandering or a stay en route.

The story explicitly sets out to illustrate R. Zeev of Zbarazh's boundless innocence and simplicity (תמימותו ופשטותו), shown when he goes to court to plead for the orphaned servant against his own wife, so a virtue is the story's point.
At the Besht's grave, R. Nahman sees the Besht standing beside him and speaking, commanding him to travel to the Land of Israel, which is a direct supernatural disclosure.

The Besht becomes invisible to a noble who had vowed to kill him, a discrete supernatural event with a clear outcome (the noble decides to reconcile), though it reads partly as an innate power rather than a one-time miracle.

The Besht secludes himself in a rock hut across the Prut, eats one meal a week and 'fasted thus for several years' away from his wife, and immerses in the mikveh even in Tevet: clear, explicit ascetic practice.
The Besht touches a tree with his finger and it bursts into flame so the freezing travelers can warm themselves, a discrete supernatural event with a clear before and after for the recipients.

A childless man receives the Besht's blessing on the condition that the children have defects, and three hunchbacked sons are born, so this is a miraculous birth of the barren-couple type, though it is only stated in summary.

The opposing litigant is explicitly described as very angry ('חרה לו מאוד') and shouting for the oath to be carried out, though his anger is the background to the tsadik's teaching rather than its subject.

The story centers on a wandering preacher (בעל דרשן) and quotes at length the tsaddik's exegesis of the Talmudic dictum on the good guest (אורח טוב, with a play on כל מה שטרח), a Torah teaching delivered at the meal.
R. Nahman, visiting the Besht's grave while awake, says he saw the dead Besht standing beside him and speaking to him (unseen by R. Yosef), which is a waking supernatural sight.

The story demonstrates the innkeeper's trust in God as it happens, and the wagon driver's explanation of the payment is simply the outcome, not a belated realization about a character's hidden identity or an event's concealed meaning.

The story centres on taking up leadership: at the circumcision feast the wandering tzaddikim mock-proclaim R. Mordechai rav of Nishchiz and R. Yaakov shatz of Zaslav, R. Mordechai is then installed as av beit din and revealed so that crowds flock to him, while the Saba refuses any appointment until he too is revealed and settles in Shpola.
The story turns on the explicit halakhic prohibition 'אסור להתפלל אחורי רבו', which the young R. Shalom considers and which R. Uri then affirms, saying he did transgress it by praying behind him.

The Besht lodges at R. Shmeril's house during his travels, and the blessing for a son happens on the eve of his departure, so the story turns on the tsaddik's stay en route (Shmeril's later trips to the Besht are a separate travel_to_the_tsaddik element).
The Besht travels to Brody via Horodenka, picks up R. Meir as a companion, lodges at an inn like a merchant, and the story turns on his spending his money there before continuing on his way.
The story is set at a gathering of the Council of Four Lands (אסיפת ד׳ ארצות), a famous historical assembly, and that gathering is where the Besht is summoned and tested.

The story's declared purpose is moral instruction in the virtue of trust in God: the Besht is sent 'to learn the trait of bitachon and teach the people to take musar', and it closes with the explicit lesson 'see how great is the power of bitachon', an exemplary tale about a simple righteous villager.

The duke (local ruler) decrees destruction of the Jews, community leaders bring the confessor to the city official, and the duke and judges interrogate and execute him, so interaction with state authorities drives the plot.

The conflict takes place in the communal prayer hall: Zusman prays in a private room inside the בית המדרש, and his wife threatens to close 'your בהמ"ד', so the beit midrash is a real setting, though here it serves as a house of prayer rather than of study.
The tzaddik's puzzling order to send the young man home gains its hidden meaning only afterward, when he reveals he had foreseen the man's death decree, which the hasidim's l'chaim toasts annulled.

The only women are the Lutsk rabbi's wife, whose childbirth sets up the story (closer to catalyst or mention), and the shochet's daughter-in-law, who is only found in his bed and never acts or speaks, so neither has a small role in which she acts.

R. Shmeril is explicitly overcome by shame (מפני הבושה, ובוש ממנו) and twice cannot ask the Besht for a son, and this drives the plot, though it is bashfulness rather than being publicly shamed as a consequence.

The anti-Jewish bishop is exposed and humiliated as a consequence of his persecution: he falls begging at the tailor's feet, is held under explicit threat of having 'חרפתו... בשתו וכלימתו' revealed, and finally confesses his wrongdoing publicly while fainting before his congregation.

The Besht uses a transmigration parable to reveal the Rishe magnate's past-life and present sin, bringing him to cry out in repentance and ask whether a tikkun remains, and the Besht then prescribes the repair of appeasing the dead pauper's children.
The tax-farmer's death is depicted directly: he wakes with a severe headache at night, says the viduy with R. Yaakov, and is found dead, fulfilling the Besht's prediction.
After the rescue, the Jews stop at an inn and pour a cup of spirits (ויסכו כוס יין שרף) for the gentile peasant as thanks, so drinking is depicted, though only as a brief detail.

R. Moshe Leib tells the leaseholder that he will win the whole estate at next week's auction, and the plot is the fulfilment of that prediction against all odds, though it reads equally as a pidyon/blessing story.

The story digresses on the tefillin knot, which the Rav devised 'according to din' so that the mitzvah of 'וקשרתם' is fulfilled by tying it daily; the Rosh knot and the wrapping direction also differ by custom, so a halakhic principle justifies a practice, even though the main plot is espionage.
The rebbe drinks a l'chaim toast at the meal, and the preacher is given spirits (י"ש), gets drunk and, emboldened, starts the dispute, so the drinking drives the plot and the lesson.

The boy's deceased grandfather carries him through the window across villages and towns, covering a month's journey in a single night, which is explicit kefitzat ha-derekh brought about by the tsaddik's prayer.

The Besht sends the narrator's father-in-law to exorcise a madman, and that night 'the spirit' (הרוח) terrifies him; he strikes it, and his fingernails fall out. An evil spirit is directly depicted, though it may be a possessing spirit (dybbuk) rather than a classic shed.

The story depicts the Besht's fixed custom of lying down after Havdalah on Motzaei Shabbat, smoking his pipe and recounting what he had seen during Shabbat; this is a tsaddik's storytelling on a set occasion, though the recounting is of visions rather than tales.

The Besht lodges with R. Shmeril while travelling, and the blessing for a son, given just before his departure, is the turning point of the story; Shmeril's later trips to the Besht are a secondary travel-to-the-tsaddik element.

Although the story is mainly a ghost/soul-tikkun narrative, it contains a discrete wonder: the Maggid's staff instantly removes the servant's fear ('כהרף עין') so he can escort the dead man, a before/after supernatural intervention on a recipient.

The story only notes in passing that R' Gershon 'said words of Torah' at the sick man's bedside, with no content given, and the Besht's explanation is a narrated account of his miracle, not a homily or exegesis.

Both stories are about testing the Besht's legitimacy, and the Besht explains that his anger at the servant mystically saved a distant Jew from robbers, depicting the tsaddik's power to act on others' behalf, while R. Yehiel's emissary ends by drawing close to the Besht.
The disciples belatedly realize the porter is a dead wandering soul (they see his shrouds) and only then understand the hidden purpose of the rabbi's trips to the fairs.

The rabbi tells the nagid's son-in-law to wait in Vienna, but he secretly follows him to the duke's palace, earning a rebuke for entering mortal danger and needing the rabbi's protection (holding his belt) to survive.

While awake, the Besht sees the demonic klipah appear as a huge Cossack by the gate, shrinking and vanishing as he approaches, and the household sees the spirit rolling like a whirlwind from corner to corner.
The tailor, sent by Elijah, passes his kerchief over the Ostroh rabbi's face, and the rabbi sees Elijah the Prophet in a revelation and faints from fear.

The rebbe explicitly argues that one cannot overcome the evil inclination ('war of Amalek') alone but only through the tsaddik, so every generation must travel to its tsaddik as Jethro came to Moses, which is a direct statement of the doctrine of cleaving to the tsaddik.

The Besht foretells that the rich man will have children only if they are born with defects, and the story closes with three hunchbacked sons; this reads as much as a conditional blessing for children as a prophecy, and the bed episode is clairvoyance rather than prediction.

The story's point is to praise Rabbi Nachman's heartfelt, heart-breaking prayer, which the Besht endorses as defining true prayer wherever he went, so it illustrates a tzaddik's devotional virtue rather than recounting a miracle.

R. Shmeril's wife is summoned and comes before the Besht, who addresses her directly, and she bears the son; the household women also leave the house and cook. These are small but active roles in a story centred on the men.
Shabbat is only incidental (a moral reminder at seudah shlishit, nail-cutting every Friday); the story centers on the Besht's vision and the scribe's exorcism injury, not on Shabbat.

In the dream, R. Gershon first takes the preaching figure for his late brother and only on drawing near realizes it is a kelipah in disguise; the later discovery of the coins and the wrapped hairs retroactively confirms the dream's truth.

The Stolin merchant does not realize he is speaking to the disguised Tsar Paul, and R. Shaul is puzzled by the rebbe's remark that Paul 'is no longer a tsar' until the assassination thirty days later reveals its hidden meaning; neither realization is narrated explicitly, so the fit is implied rather than certain.
The mysterious host in the forest is revealed as the prophet Jonah ben Amittai, a supernatural figure, not a concealed living tzaddik or lamed-vavnik, so the nistar likeness is only superficial.

The Besht tries to shield the Pavlysh blood-libel victims through prayer and assurances (heaven promised to annul the decree), but the attempt fails and the story centres on mourning and the martyrs' refusal of vengeance.
The text is a pure exegetical teaching on Psalms 114 built on wordplay and acronyms (notarikon) attributed to the rabbi, and it has no narrated events.

The story has a dybbuk, the Besht's warning against using holy names before age 36, his exorcism threat, his prayer for rain and the gentiles' idol procession, but none of these is sorcery by witches, non-Jewish magicians or forbidden Jewish practice.

No explicit religious prohibition is invoked or violated; the Besht's weeping 'disturbing the Sabbath' and the martyrs' plea that he retract his decree of revenge are only faint, implicit associations with prohibition.

The story clearly exists to illustrate the virtue of faith (bitachon), but that virtue belongs to an anonymous old innkeeper the Besht is sent to learn from, not to a tzaddik, so the tag fits only if it is read loosely to cover exemplary laymen.

The plot is driven by fulfilled predictions: the dying rabbi foretells that the next person to die will name his successor, and the hidden-tzaddik tailor foretells that the Ostroh rabbi will refuse until told of the tailor's command, and both come true.

A dead debtor who never repaid his loan is sentenced by Heaven ('נפסק דינו') to be reincarnated as a horse and do hard labor for his creditor, which is a heavenly punishment, though the story frames it more as working off a debt than as retribution for sin.

Rabbi Nachman rebukes his own followers (anash) and, through a parable, teaches them their proper place: they must not meddle in disputes between tzaddikim, though the story's main theme is the controversy among masters itself.
At the Baal Shem Tov's grave, R' Nahman sees the Besht standing beside him and speaking to him, while R' Yosef, who was with him, perceives nothing.
The story shows R. Zvi Yehuda's supernatural holiness: impurity flees from him and his clothes stay pristine, which is a sanctity or purity motif rather than an ethical virtue being illustrated.
The Besht's trip to Gan Eden reads as a soul-ascent and the spirit frightens the scribe 'בתוך שנתו' (in his sleep), so no waking-state supernatural sight is clearly depicted.

The story shows the Besht's visionary perception of a pillar of Torah-light and R. Shimshon's spiritual tikkun, but it presents no kabbalistic doctrine or hidden teaching for initiates, so it fits visions or supernatural sight rather than esoteric knowledge.

The Besht's knowledge of the rabbi's hidden flaw (the cross appearing before him during the Shema) is clairvoyance or holy-spirit insight, and the rabbi's intrusive image is a spiritual affliction; neither is a giluy, a direct mystical disclosure granted to a character.

The story features idolatrous teraphim and impurity, but no character is warned against or violates a specific religious prohibition; the boy is an abducted victim rescued by prayer, so prohibition is only an incidental background association.

The Besht gives away the gold coin to the kloyz and the poor out of trust in God (he still 'brought money home'), which is about charity and bitachon rather than poverty embraced as a virtue or a refusal of wealth.

The story shows the tzaddik's hidden power and foresight in testing the young man and arranging his match by dream and illness, so it is a wonder/matchmaking tale rather than one illustrating his virtues such as humility, charity or faith.
The text is a pure homiletic interpretation of a verse ('רב לכם סוב את ההר הזה') using wordplay and acronym exegesis about the evil inclination, with no narrated events.
The story only notes in passing that the Spoler Zeide was born in a village, and a circumcision feast serves as a setting; no birth is depicted as an event.

The story centres on R. Shmeril's ongoing relationship with the Besht: he hosts him, is too ashamed to ask for a blessing, regularly travels to him for amulets and gives him gifts, and the Besht chooses a son over wealth on his behalf. He is a devoted follower rather than a formal disciple, hence medium confidence.
The only figure called a baal shem is the Besht himself (the story's objection to the title 'baal shem' concerns him), and no other non-Besht baal shem appears.

The mikveh appears only in one passing clause (the Besht went to the mikveh and wept on Erev Shabbat); the actual scenes, the bitter prayers and the night vision with R. Akiva and the martyrs, take place in the prayer setting and the Besht's room.

While awake during Shalom Aleichem, the Besht turns to the door as if seeing something, and later explains that Samael (the Satan) came to snatch the preacher and he rebuked him; this is a waking supernatural sight, whereas the rabbi's sighting of the Besht happens in a dream.
A non-Jewish witch (מכשפה/כשפנית) with a demon works sorcery to stop the rain and sends the demon against the Besht, so she is a central character.

The plot is driven by Shmeril's wish for a son and the Besht's blessing; the wife is summoned, addressed and gives birth, which makes her a minor participant rather than the woman who triggers the events.

Samael (הס"מ) actively appears at the door during Shalom Aleichem trying to snatch the preacher, and the Besht rebukes and fends him off; this is an on-scene evil spirit, though he is the Satan figure rather than generic שדים/מזיקים.

The only related wording is the idiom 'בחרדת שמחה' (joyful awe) when the hasid greets the tzaddik, and the rich man's 'אימה' is suspicion of a trick; no one physically trembles as a religious or supernatural response.

The plot is driven by Shmeril's wish for a son, not by the wife; she is summoned, addressed directly by the Besht and bears the son, which makes her a minor participating character rather than a catalyst (the women vacating the house is incidental).

The story centres on the dead disciple's experience in Gan Eden, where he cannot find a place until the Besht explains why, which fits the tag's world-to-come (afterlife) sense, though not messianic or end-times eschatology.
The story is about appointing a successor to Lublin's communal rabbinate (the Rav of Ostroh, named by a hidden-tzaddik tailor), not about one Hasidic rebbe's leadership passing to the next.

The story is a homiletic gematria/acronym reading of Psalm 114 about redemption, and the closing formula 'זכותו יגן עלינו' is a stock blessing rather than a depiction of a tsaddik protecting anyone from a specific harm.
The story illustrates a specific virtue, humility (R. Shmelke guarding against pride at his reception in Nikolsburg), not a general or unspecified virtue, so a humility-specific tag fits better.

This is a full narrative of a hidden-tzaddik tailor, the Lublin rabbinic succession and an Elijah revelation, with only a short bibliographic preface and a brief concluding explanation, not a homiletic frame.

R. Avraham Abba, who suspected the Besht of being an ignoramus, realizes only after the Besht reveals his hidden lapse and the hidden sin tied to the bed that the Besht truly has holy spirit, though this reads more as a skeptic convinced by a test than a classic belated unmasking.

The demon turns its face to the wall because, as the Besht explains, 'נתבייש ממני', so shame is explicitly depicted as a spiritual response to the tzaddik's presence, though the subject is a demon rather than a human character.

The only related word is 'חרדו מאוד' (Rabbi Yaakov Yosef's men were very afraid he would punish Menachem Mendel), which expresses social fear of the tzaddik rather than an actual depiction of physical trembling as a religious or supernatural response.
The story is about the Besht's clairvoyance and the specific fault of doubting tzaddikim (faith in the righteous and honoring them), not a general or unspecified virtue.

The story is an exegetical praise of the tzaddik's holiness, in which impurity (niddah/keri) flees from him; it is about purity, and no character is forbidden from doing something or breaks a prohibition.

The story shows specific virtues, charity (giving the gold coin to the kloyz and the poor) and trust in God despite having no money for expenses, rather than an unspecified virtue, so more specific tags fit better than the general 'virtues' tag.

The story has no witchcraft or sorcery: the only supernatural elements are the tzaddikim staying hidden under the bed (ransomed with eggs and produce) and miracles by holy men, which are not forbidden magic.

The plot turns on the Seer of Lublin's dealings with a young follower who defies the Seer's order to go home, so the rebbe-hasid relationship is central, though the story's stated moral is the power of ten hasidim together.
The otherworldly setting shown is Gan Eden (the lower paradise synagogue and the heavenly court); Gehinnom is only named as the place the opponent was expelled to, never depicted as a setting.
The story centers on the rabbi's direct dealings with Tsar Paul, who imprisons him, and Tsar Alexander, who frees him, favors him, and consults him about his father's murderers.
The story is about a tsaddik whose holiness repels impurity (miraculously whitened garments in an aggadic reading); it contains no sorcery, witchcraft, or forbidden magical practice.

The story centers on a litigant who lies in court and is about to swear falsely, a violation of the prohibition against false claims and oaths, and the death of his child is the consequence that brings him to confess, although the word אסור never appears.
The Besht's blessing with his staff and the amulets (קמיע) he gives are sanctioned tzaddik wonder-working, not sorcery by witches, non-Jewish magicians, or forbidden Jewish practices.

R. Nachman directly rebukes people who were slandering the Besht, which reads as a confrontation with opponents of Hasidism, though the parable about disputes among great men could also mean these are ordinary followers meddling in a quarrel between tzaddikim rather than mitnagdim.

The villain is called 'זד יהיר' (arrogant evildoer), but that is a stock epithet; the story is about lust, a forged divorce (get) and the tzaddik's exposure of the fraud, not arrogance as a moral theme.

The story centers on a blood libel. The Besht struggles against the accuser ('the persecutor called Stiegator'), ordering the martyrs' souls to take vengeance on him, and a Brody preacher who stirred strife is blamed for the captives' deaths.
R. Shmelke's arrival as rabbi of Nikolsburg shows his humility toward the townspeople, but the story depicts no opposition, mitnagdim or maskilim, and no Hasidic vs. non-Hasidic tension.

The word 'pidyon' appears only in the grandfather's remark that eggs and produce under the bed acted as a ransom hiding the rabbis from a mob, not in a tsaddik averting death or a heavenly decree, or a pidyon payment given to a tsaddik.
The wife's weeping and the husband's grief (יגון) are plot-driven reactions to the abandonment and the forged get, not a theme of sadness or melancholy (עצבות) treated as a spiritual problem.

The arc is the tzaddik actively arranging a match through instructions, a demanded loan, and supernatural pressure on the bride, not an explicit prophecy that is later fulfilled; his foreknowledge is only implied.

The son's wildness is implicitly tied to the father's failure to notify the Besht, but the story never frames it as a punishment; it is a consequence that the Besht then corrects, so the story is about remedy rather than retribution.

The story turns on a hasid's unwavering trust in his rebbe, the Seer of Lublin: the hasid stakes the wager on the rebbe's clairvoyance, the rebbe seems to snub him, and then vindicates him by exposing the wealthy scoffer and warmly greeting the disciple.

The rabbi, through his dream, recognizes that the uncle's deathbed prophecy about 'Israel son of the midwife' was the Besht and accepts him; the preacher later learns that the Besht's odd turning during 'Shalom Aleichem' was driving off Samael to save him, a hidden meaning he had misread out of pride.

No character clearly lies or deceives: the story is about a scoffer who slanders the Seer of Lublin and tests him, and the Seer's seemingly warm welcome is a lesson rather than a lie (the hasid's speech calling slanderers' words 'lies' is only a borderline link).

The protagonist is explicitly called 'הארינדאר המוכסן' (the arendar/leaseholder); he brings his daughter and her groom to the Belzer rebbe, and his wife's requests about cows, milk and grain fit an arendar's livelihood.

The tzaddik's role is clairvoyant discernment (seeing that the get is forged and the match invalid) and staging a trap that exposes the fraud, not a prophecy about a future event that comes true. His remark that the woman will not end up with the messenger is incidental to the plot.

The boy's status as a prodigy and the Maharal's pupil, his sharp derasha at the engagement, and the room of books are only background; the story is about the kidnapping, the teraphim head and the rescue through prayer, not about Torah study as an activity.

The story shows the Shekhinah resting on the Besht in prayer, so that water, grain and people around him tremble, and he has a supernatural sight of Samael gathering prayers at dawn; this is direct mystical disclosure, though it partly overlaps with 'visions'.

The Besht's puzzling order to pay the 'debt' turns out to produce exactly the 200-gold dowry, but no character is shown belatedly grasping the truth: the lord simply recalculates, Reb Leib is just puzzled, and the Besht already knew.

The gevir's daughter, turned against her husband by malicious neighbor women, drives the plot: her quarrel makes him flee, her lament pushes her father to act, and the suitor's desire for her leads to the forged divorce, while the Tzaddik and the men are the central actors.

The Besht predicts several times that the accused will be saved, but they are killed, so the story shows a failed prediction (later explained by heaven concealing the decree), not a prediction that comes true.

This is a miracle and clairvoyance tale: the Belz tzaddik foresees the danger, urges confession, finds the lost horses and sends the gentile in a dream to rescue the travellers, so its point is his supernatural power and faith in tzaddikim rather than his ethical virtues.

The Besht reveals the rich man's past deeds and previous incarnation (clairvoyance, not prediction), and R. Shalom of Kaminka's claim that the woman's money is lost is a pessimistic judgment whose fulfilment the story never shows.

The only woman is the biblical Shunammite, and she appears inside the tzaddik's sermon on a rabbinic saying rather than as a participant in the Hasidic story, so 'mention_only' fits better than 'minor_character', even though she acts within the sermon.

Rabbi Shimshon of Vienna declares that the new match 'will not stand' and the get is false, and tells the husband 'all will come to its place in peace', and both come true at the wedding, though the story leans more on clairvoyant insight than on explicit forecasting.

The story centers on the Besht's grief over the Pavlitch martyrs and his encounter with their souls; R. David of Korostyshev and the 'אנשי סגולתו' appear only as observers, and no master-disciple relationship is developed.

The Ostroh rabbi falls on his face and faints 'מרוב הפחד והמורא' when shown Elijah the Prophet, and later tears his garments and obeys the hidden tzaddik-tailor's command, which depicts religious awe of a holy figure, though the object of awe is Elijah rather than God or a tzaddik proper.

The Rebbe of Liadi is in direct conflict with Tsar Paul, who has him arrested and imprisoned for life out of suspicion; the story also mentions earlier denunciation by Avigdor and ongoing Jewish opponents ('הפיקו לו מצוקים מבני עמינו').
The innkeeper's wife is referred to (he tells her about the rebbe, and she falls ill and is promised healing) and Sarah is named in 'Leib ben Sarah', but no woman speaks or acts in the plot.
The story features prophetic dreams, Samael trying to snatch the preacher, and the Besht's protective prayer, but no witchcraft, sorcery, or forbidden magical practice.

The narrator says he recorded the Rav of Polonne's custom of touching his tefillin right after the prayer in order to learn alacrity (zerizut) in divine service, so the story explicitly illustrates a virtue, though a specific one rather than a general virtue.

The boy's good mood ('בדיחא דעתו') after studying is only a brief detail, and it is presented as self-satisfaction and pride rather than religious joy; the story is about humility and the Besht's tale foretelling Menachem Mendel's life.

The Besht's prolonged prayer, described as standing, trembling and making bodily movements (עומד ורועד ועשית כתנועותיך), depicts ecstatic fervor, though the story's focus is his mystical work raising souls of the dead (tikkun) rather than enthusiasm itself.

The story mainly shows the tzaddik's clairvoyance (ruach ha-kodesh) and cleverness in exposing a forged get, which makes it a wonder/justice tale rather than an illustration of virtues such as humility, charity or faith, though the opening does praise his wisdom and holiness.

The Besht orders everyone out and the sick disciple to keep their talk secret, yet a boy hides and reveals it and the disciple confirms it; separately, his unkept handshake vow costs him a place in Gan Eden, so disobedience with consequences is present, though it is not the story's central focus.

The story centres on Leib Sarah's miraculous shortened journey (kefitzat ha-derekh) to Vienna and his secret visit to the duke; his virtue of secretly supporting hidden tzaddikim appears only in a parenthetical aside and is not the story's point.

The Besht does foresee the disciple's death and promises him Gan Eden, but the story turns on his clairvoyance about a hidden sin and a dream report of his heavenly standing, not on a prophecy shown to come true.

The triggering event, the dayan cursing the Mokhiah while he leads prayers, explicitly happens on Shabbat, and the confrontation is pointedly held over until the day after Shabbat, though the climax itself falls on Sunday.
The story covers tefillin knots, a hasidic spy in the Vilna Gaon's study house, and the translation of the Rav's defense, and no recitation of Psalms is depicted.

The Seer of Lublin foresaw by divine inspiration that the young man was fated to die on the holiday, but the hasidim's toasts annulled the decree, so the foreseen event never happened; this is clairvoyant perception of a decree, not a prediction that comes true.

The merchant's barren wife is referred to (the Besht's promise that she will bear a son, and the report that she did) and the host mentions an 'אשה עצורה', but no woman speaks or acts in the narrative.

The son weeps at his father's deathbed, but this is incidental grief, not sadness/melancholy (עצבות) treated as a spiritual problem; the story concerns the Besht's celibacy, his son's holy soul, and transmitting a divine name.

A dayan is brought to Polonne to stand against the Mokhiach and curses him. In the ensuing quarrel his tefillin are shown to be invalid and he is exposed as ignorant and flees, so this is a rivalry with a tzaddik that ends in the rival's defeat, though it is more hostility than a contest of powers.

The story shows the Besht's disapproval of an unauthorized and distorted written record of his teachings, but no religious or moral prohibition (אסור) is stated, given, or violated; the point is about faulty transmission, not a forbidden act.

R. Nahman delivers a brief rebuking parable (mashal) to detractors of the Besht, an incidental use of a parable in argument rather than a depicted practice of storytelling at a gathering, meal, set occasion or as a theurgic act.

The plot turns on the rich man's wife, a non-Hasidic Jew who scorns the Besht and mocks the holy names; he demonstrates their power and then rebukes and punishes her for her skepticism, which is an oppositional encounter even though she is not formally a mitnaged or maskil.

This is the Besht's revelation (hitgalut) narrative: while he is still a hidden, scorned figure, a possessed woman publicly exposes him before Rabbi Gershon and the Kitov hasidim, and from then on he is recognized, taken up as a melamed, and eventually takes on followers.

Shabbat appears only as the incidental setting (seudah shlishit after the derashah) where the Ostroh rabbi tells the tailor's secret; the story itself is about the hidden-tzaddik tailor and the rabbinic succession, not about Shabbat.

The hidden-tzaddik tailor delivers a message from Elijah the Prophet, who is invisible to others, and the Ostroh rabbi briefly sees Elijah when the tailor passes his handkerchief over his face, though the rabbi faints and never speaks with Elijah himself.

The Besht foretells that Starograd will burn piecemeal, quarter by quarter, and that those under decree will die by killing and plague, and the narrator confirms each prediction came true (וכן הי׳ שנשרף בכמה פעמים...).

The story centers on the Besht's ecstatic trembling in prayer; the last episode, where he steers prayers away from Samael and shames R. David to keep out alien thoughts, guards the community's prayers rather than rescuing a person from illness, authorities or demons.

The story turns on master-disciple ties: the Besht, from his grave, commands his disciple R. Nahman to go to the Land of Israel, and R. Mendel of Peremyshlany attends R. Nahman, receives teachings from him, and is at his deathbed, though it also covers peer tensions with the Mokhiah.
A wealthy man who refused to visit the Besht and dismissed his promise as empty words or chance is won over by the miraculous events and ends by rushing to the Besht to report everything.

The story shows a rabbi clashing with a wealthy householder's wife over synagogue prayer timing, a communal or class dispute, and nothing marks the couple as mitnagdim, maskilim or opponents of Hasidism.

The story centres on kefitzat ha-derekh (the magical journey to Vienna) and invisibility before the duke's guards; the only hint of perception is that the rebbe 'sensed' the son-in-law secretly following him, which is incidental and could be ordinary noticing.

Rabbi Nachman tells a brief mashal (parable) to rebuke people who spoke against the Besht, which is didactic parable use, not a depicted storytelling practice at a gathering, set occasion, or as a spiritual/theurgic act.

The story centres on a visionary visit by the departed Baal Shem Tov and the Maggid, who confirm that a Torah teaching on the haftarah was faithfully transmitted; it never depicts kabbalistic or secret doctrine as such, so the link to esoteric knowledge is only incidental.

This is a pre-Hasidic tale about a hidden righteous tailor who names Lublin's next rabbi, but nowhere is it framed as a lesson in a particular virtue such as humility, charity or hospitality; its stated purpose is only to pass on a true and wondrous story.

Rabbi Leib Sarahs secretly travels each Friday to Vienna, enters the duke's palace unseen by the guards, and talks with the duke at length once he wakes, which is a direct interaction with a non-Jewish ruler.
The community is saved from the bishop's persecution by its own fasting and prayer and by an ordinary Jewish tailor's ruse, not by a tsaddik's shielding intervention.

The only shochet is the narrator, who notes in passing that he was a shochet in Tulchin when he heard the story; his occupation plays no part in the plot, which centres on the Besht's trembling prayer and R. David the prayer leader.

The only 'disclosure' is the bishop's staged claim, under pressure from the tailor's ruse, that Muhammad rebuked him; the narrative treats his flights to Muhammad as a deception, so no character genuinely receives a mystical revelation.

The story centers on the Besht as a concealed mystic: heaven forbade him to use the holy names (practical Kabbalah) until age thirty-six, a possessed woman reveals this secret, and he performs a yichud against the impure forces, so the esoteric dimension is substantive, not incidental.
The story is a homiletic teaching about despising honor and respecting one's fellow (הזהרו בכבוד חבריכם); it is moral exhortation, not a religious prohibition being imposed or violated.

The Besht's Zohar recitation is only a passing scene detail, and the story centres on clairvoyance, prayer in the mikveh and a heavenly reply about a blood libel, not on kabbalistic doctrine or initiate knowledge.

The Riga magnate does give the Besht a pidyon, but explicitly with no request, and the Besht reveals a sin and prescribes repentance (appeasing the dead man's sons) rather than averting a death or heavenly decree.

The Chabad disciples take R. Aaron of Karlin for an ordinary man whose acts are 'simple', until he reads their thoughts and reveals the hidden holiness behind his eating and secular speech; the story never shows the disciples' own reaction, so their realization is implied rather than stated.
The story concerns the Rav of Raszków, the Besht, a preacher (mokhiah) and the city of Shargorod's fate, with no depiction of mitnagdim, maskilim or opposition to Hasidism.

The kloyz and the great beit midrash come up only when the parnas explains the preaching custom; the actual preaching takes place in the great synagogue (בה"כ הגדולה), so no study hall is a setting in the story.
Psalms 95 and 92 ('לכו נרננה', 'מזמור שיר ליום השבת') appear only as fixed Kabbalat Shabbat liturgy that R. Aharon leads in the afterlife, not as Tehillim recitation for devotion or intercession.

The rabbi had undertaken a long series of fasts (פ' תענית) to rid himself of a disturbing thought during Shema; the Besht cites this as proof and replaces the fasting with a different remedy, so ascetic fasting is a real plot element, though secondary.
The Besht's blessing, threat with his staff, and amulets (kamia) are holy-man wonder-working, not sorcery by witches, gentile magicians, or forbidden Jewish practices.

The merchant unknowingly spends Shabbat with, and is repaid by, the prophet Jonah ben Amittai in a vanishing forest house, which is a supernatural appearance akin to giluy Eliyahu that the Besht identifies at the end, though the character does not recognize it as a revelation while it happens.

The story centres on the Besht's use of holy names, which heaven forbade him until he was 33. It also shows him threatening to expel a spirit from a madwoman, confining demons in an impure house through a yichud, and healing a madman, all mystical means used for concrete results.
The woman lost money she lent to a business partner who vanished and died; he was not her husband, so there is no aguna, and the story concerns debt and reincarnation, not release for remarriage.

On his deathbed the Besht says the heavens trembled when his son Zvi was conceived and that he could have drawn down Adam's soul, but this is a passing mystical boast about a holy soul, not a miraculous conception overcoming barrenness or achieved through a blessing.

The story praises the judicial wonder-power of an unidentified 'R. Yitzhak' (possibly an early figure like R. Yitzhak of Drohobych, near the Besht's circle), and nothing in the text clearly marks him as an earlier or non-Hasidic sage.
Central plot: R. Yitzhak perceives that a man's tefillin are invalid, they are examined and found invalid since being written, and he writes him new, uniquely holy tefillin.

The plot turns on teacher-disciple bonds: the sick student's obligation to his rabbis (Ze'ev Kitzes and David Purkes) conflicts with the Besht's charge, and the story ends with those rabbis drawing close to the Besht as his followers, though they are pre-Hasidic 'hasidim' rather than rebbes in the strict sense.

The rebbe knows on his own that the horse is the reincarnation of the dead debtor, picks out exactly that one debt note, and foresees the horse's death once the debt is forgiven, which is knowledge no one could have by ordinary means.

R. Nahman explicitly teaches that no one escapes alien thoughts in prayer, noting even the subtle thought of wanting to finish the prayer is a מחשבה זרה that creates an accuser, a direct teaching on alien thoughts during devotion.

Beyond the Maggid–disciple frame, the story centres on a peer encounter between the adult R. Menachem Mendel and R. Yaakov Yosef of Polonne, including the warnings of R. Menachem Mendel's companions and the questions of R. Yaakov Yosef's followers, which is substantive interaction among Hasidim.
The story centres on the martyrdom of the Pavolitch blood-libel victims ("כשנהרגו"), whose killing, torture, and afterlife testimony as kedoshim are depicted events that drive the plot.

When R' Michel of Zlotchov lays his hands on the disguised Saba's head he immediately senses his hidden holiness and sends men to find him, and the Saba later explains the unseen reason (eggs and produce as a pidyon) why the searchers did not find them under the bed.

The maggid R. Yitzhak Drabizner clashes with the tax-farmer's wife and husband (curse, death of child, exchange of threatening letters, the tax-farmer's death), escalating into a town-wide dispute (מחלוקת) whose opponents die, including the local rabbi who reconciles.

The martyrs' account depicts action set in the upper worlds: an uproar in Gan Eden, souls fleeing through the heikhalot to a higher heikhal, and their entry into Gan Eden after half an hour of Gehenna. The main scene, however, takes place in the Besht's room, and his ascent is only implied.

The dying rabbi foreknows that the hidden-tzaddik tailor will die next and will name his successor, the tailor foresees the Ostraha rabbi's refusal, and the tailor makes the Ostraha rabbi see the prophet Elijah by passing his handkerchief over his face.

The Besht is shown raging at his servant on the Sabbath, which troubles the visiting observer, and he grows angry again when told of the doubt, so anger is the story's central moral problem even though it is finally justified.
Rabbi Uri of Strelisk publicly answers the young Shalom of Belz's unspoken thoughts about testing him, and the narrator explicitly concludes he is 'יודע מחשבות' (a reader of thoughts).

The deceased disciple sees the living Besht teaching Torah in a heavenly palace of Gan Eden, the same teaching he later gives on earth, and the story closes by explicitly mentioning the Besht's 'עליות נשמה' (soul ascents).
The Besht perceives from afar the ascent of a righteous man's soul and recognizes him as the Konstantin rabbinic decisor, knowledge he could not have by natural means.

The story explicitly shows the rabbi putting on tefillin for the field Minhah (an unusual custom), in contrast to R. Nahman praying without tallit and tefillin, though it is a passing detail rather than the story's focus.

Clothing carries religious and social meaning throughout the story: the Maggid reads the boy's hat worn askew as pride, Menahem Mendel is said to have been always distinguished in his dress, and his visit to the Toldot without hat or belt, wearing silver-buckled shoes, is explained as humility hidden beneath an outward garment of pride.

The story is about trust in God (bitachon) and the innkeeper's partnership with God; his praying right at dawn is mentioned only as a passing trait, and his weeping in the field is spontaneous plea, not liturgy.

The deceased R. Aharon describes reciting Mincha and leading Kabbalat Shabbat (Lekhu Neranenah, Mizmor Shir le-Yom ha-Shabbat) before the ark in the heavenly synagogue, which is a central depicted liturgical scene.

The Besht drives off Samael, who sought to 'snatch' the preacher (i.e., take his life), by rebuking him and praying, and then labors until the preacher and his household recover from illness, though the death threat is implied rather than explicit.

Rabbi David flees in fear of a blood libel as notable men 'היו מתפחדים' of being accused, and the souls in heaven flee in panic 'כמפני חרב' at the Besht's weeping, so fear of danger is explicitly depicted.

In the final episode R. David, humiliated by the Besht before Yom Kippur prayers and fearing he had been seen as sinful, learns afterward that the insult was meant to break his heart and protect the prayers from Satan, so he grasps the event's hidden meaning only in hindsight.

The Besht heals a blind boy by whispering holy names into his ear and explicitly does so to show 'the power of the holiness of the Name' to the wife who mocked healing by שמות הקדושים, so the healing is a name-based practical feat.

The Besht is shown praying at length after the synagogue service, and the plot turns on the rabbi's kavanah during the recitation of Shema Yisrael, so liturgical prayer is depicted and central to the story.
The orphaned maidservant is a peripheral woman who takes part in the quarrel that drives the story; the rebbetzin, who speaks and acts more, may fit a catalyst or major tag better.
