The Besht confronts a visiting rabbi who belittles him and whose spiritual flaw is doubting great tzaddikim; the townspeople also disregard the Besht, and the rabbi is won over and honors him, a central opponent-turned-admirer encounter even though the word 'mitnagdim' is never used.
The story explicitly depicts the tsaddik's ecstatic dancing (ריקודו) on Sabbaths and festivals, light on his feet like a four-year-old, moving all onlookers to repentance.
The Besht directly opposes a non-Jewish witch who blocks the rain with sorcery and sends her demon against him, and he defeats and imprisons the demon.

The core of the story is the Besht's deathbed scene on the day he dies, where he speaks his last words to his son Zvi and passes on a divine name so they can keep studying together after his death; the opening about his wife's death is only a brief lead-in.

As a dayan, the Shpoler Zeide ruled to permit (release) an aguna against the surrounding rabbis' prohibition; the episode is brief within a longer biography but is an actual depicted act of releasing an aguna.
The attendant is gripped by great dread (אימה גדולה ופחד גדול, knees knocking) at the ghost's voice and says he is too afraid to escort the dead man until the Maggid's staff removes his fear.

The story is about the rabbi giving a tikkun to a wandering dead soul at the fair; his collecting money there for the tzaddikim is only a brief closing aside about his motives, not a depiction of almsgiving or providing for the poor.
The Besht sees a demon (mazik) in the house that the Mokhiah cannot see, and then enables the Mokhiah to see it as well, which is a clear case of supernatural perception.

The melamed is plainly shown in deep sorrow (נצטער מאד, כמבולבל מרוב הצער, ישב כמשתומם, כל היום בצער גדול) after forgetting the teaching from his dream, and the Besht's summons resolves it, though the sorrow serves the story's real theme of longing and being drawn to the Besht rather than עצבות as a spiritual flaw.

The Besht commands a sofer to write protective amulets (shmirot) for all the rooms, so a scribe appears in his professional role, though only briefly and as a functional rather than central character.

The story's premise is that R. Aharon of Karlin performed his yihudim ("פעולותיו ביחודים") in deep concealment, unlike the open yihudim the Chabad disciples knew, and this is in the kabbalistic sense; but the yihudim are only mentioned as background, never actually performed.

The Besht and the rabbi of Rashkov pray to avert heavenly decrees (fire, murder, plague) against the towns, and partly succeed in mitigating them, which is explicit communal protection through prayer.
The Spoler Zeide himself works as a village shochet u-bodek, and a drunken regional examining shochet who fails to detect a nick in the knife plays a central role in the episode.

R. Nachman of Horodenka describes immersing daily in a freezing mikveh and then sitting in a scalding one for about an hour without feeling the heat, so the mikveh is the setting of the episode he recounts, though briefly.

The melamed dreams he sees the Besht teaching Torah through a palace window and is turned away at the door, and this dream drives the plot: next day the Besht calls him and repeats the same words, which brings him close to the Besht.
The story's closing scene shows R. Nachman studying Zohar as his soul departed, a brief but deliberate depiction of Kabbalah study.

The Besht directs his disciple the Mokhiah (R. Leib) on preaching and sends him to Lemberg, appears in the rabbi's dream as 'my disciple', and protects him from Samael, so the master-disciple bond drives the story.
The story is set around the blood libel of Pavolitch (c. 1753), a real historical event whose martyrdom, the flight of R. David, and the Brody preacher's role drive the whole narrative.

The Lemberg rabbi, at first just following custom, is drawn to the Besht through a dream and his uncle's testimony: he hosts the Besht's disciple, asks him to reveal all he received from the Besht, and wants to travel to him, which is a rapprochement arc even though the disciple's own trials are the main thread.
The Besht foretells that the wife will bear a son and that Shmeril will lose his wealth, and both predictions explicitly come true ('וכן היה').

Humility is central: the boy weeps over his pride in his learning, the Besht declares him 'שפל בעיניו', he signs 'השפל באמת', and the Toldot's parable explains his outward finery as a hiding place for his true humility (ענוה בתכלית).

The story centers on a war between the Ottomans (ישמעאל) and the Greeks/Russians (יון) and the flight (הבריחה) during it, in which the town, its surroundings and Teytshilnik were destroyed, so a historical event is part of the setting.

The plot turns on the Besht telling the man to lease the arenda from the Jew-hating noble (השר), who has barred Jews from his village for fifteen years yet sends for him and grants the lease, a real interaction with a non-Jewish noble.

The story is a moral exemplum about bitachon (trust in God), but the virtue is shown by a wealthy layman whom R. Michel himself calls an 'איש פשוט' and by the traveller, not by the tzaddik, who only sends the man and explains the outcome.

No soul is actually reincarnated, but the plot turns on gilgul: the martyred souls decline to avenge themselves because revenge would require them to accept reincarnation, and they fear being spoiled in another life.

When the Besht reveals that the rabbi will forget יעלה ויבא again, the rabbi 'נתבהל מאוד' (was greatly alarmed) at the tzaddik's knowledge of hidden things, which is fear or awe of a tzaddik, though brief and not elaborated.

The Besht repeatedly predicts the Pavolitch blood-libel victims will be saved, yet they are executed, and the story explains the failure twice: heaven concealed their martyrdom lest his prayer annul a decree averting worse, and a Brody preacher's agitation brought about the killing.
The story is set at a brit milah where R. Mordechai of Chernobyl is sandak and R. Avraham the mohel, who drops the knife in awe while saying the circumcision blessing.

The town's komisar summons R' Leib and threatens to deliver him in iron chains to a distant nobleman over the Besht's ransom debt, so the plot turns on coercive officialdom; the komisar may be a magnate's estate official rather than a state functionary, hence medium confidence.
The Besht perceives, beyond any normal means, that the Kalisz tzitzit were spun with the proper intention (לשמה), which is supernatural knowledge of a hidden fact.
The Besht protects a tax-collector's household from a witchcraft-sent spirit by writing protective amulets (shmirot) in every room and driving the demonic klipah out of the house and courtyard.

The Besht says that הס"מ (Samael) tried to snatch the preacher from his house, and he rebuked him during Shalom Aleichem and bargained it down to punishment (illness) instead of death, so the Angel of Death acts as an agent in the plot.

The story shows the Besht's habit after Havdalah of lying down to rest, smoking his pipe (ועישן לולקע), and recounting what he saw on Shabbat, which is when he explains the vision. It is a habitual, framing act, though a minor detail.
Zusman's wife acts on her own: she threatens to shut the rabbi's beit midrash, and the story's climax is her punishment and death, which makes her a central actor.
The Besht foretells that the robbed Jew will soon be brought to town ('ותראה שיביאו אותו מהרה לעיר'), and the story confirms it ('וכן הי׳').

The dead R. Aharon, appearing in a dream, narrates scenes set in Gan Eden: Tektiger summoning him to the heavenly court, Tektiger's expulsion to Gehinnom, and his own Kabbalat Shabbat in a synagogue in the lower Gan Eden.
